RagShortTexts: Silver strikes at Kutná Hora funded Přemyslid expansion, turning Bohemia into Europe's mint.

Variants.Content: Silver strikes at Kutná Hora in central Bohemia set off a major industrial rush in the thirteenth century. King Ottokar II granted mining privileges to the district, and the later Ius Regale Montanorum code set out the crown's share of the ore and the rights of the miners who worked it. Skilled Saxon miners were settled in the district, and they sank shafts deep into the rock with waterwheel hoists to lift the ore. The mint produced large quantities of silver Prague groschen, a coin that became a common currency across the region. Tax on the bullion funded the royal treasury, and the miners' skills spread to other mining towns in the kingdom.

Silver bullion financed Ottokar's ambitions in the Empire. Loans went to Rhenish electors, and the wages of hired mercenary cavalry were paid from the mint. Each shipment from the Bohemian mines strengthened the Přemyslid claim to Central European leadership.
Miners wearing tallow lamps on leather caps chisel through granite ore faces underground. Smelting furnaces billow toxic smoke, yet refined ingots pour into royal casting troughs.
